claims.assertion: The trip is RydeTAXI and metered, so distance actually driven enters the fare directly; the meter charged 12.17 km of distance fare $17.16 while the optimal route is 7.2 km, confirming extra kilometres were billed to the rider.
claims.void_reason: citation check: cites 0 — not a citable clause

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows one off-route segment 09:04–09:14 in which 5.23 km were driven where the optimal route covers only 1.08 km, adding 4.15 km and reaching up to 1989 m from the optimal route — an unexcused deviation under RD-1.

No exemption applies: there is no traffic incident near the route during the trip window, the only speed-band entries are band 3 (20–29 km/h, not the congested band 1–2) on two roads, and weather was fair, so RD-4 (a) and (b) cannot excuse the segment.

There is no consent to the reroute: the complete, fully timestamped chat contains only the rider's pickup message at 08:47 and the driver's ETA reply at 08:48, both before the 09:04 segment start, and neither mentions any route or road; the driver's post-trip statement that the GPS rerouted him is a claim, not a rider message.

The rider's complaint that the driver never asked before deviating is consistent with the chat record, which shows no route-change proposal from the driver at any time before the 09:04 off-route segment began.

Under RD-2 for a metered RydeTAXI the refund is Σ(unexempted extra_km) × this trip's per-km rate = 4.15 km × $1.4100/km = $5.8515, rounded to $5.85, computed from the off-route extra distance in F4 and the per-km rate in F5.
The driver already has 1 upheld dispute in the last 90 days among 3 disputes, so with this deviation upheld the case becomes 'repeated' and warrants the additional account-review action of RD-6.

weaknesses: The GPS trace ends 4 minutes before the 09:20:45 drop-off (F1), so the final stretch of the journey is not on record — the rival reading of the missing coverage is that it shifts some of the excess distance onto unrecorded ground and may support an 'evidence insufficient / escalate' argument (G12).

There is a discrepancy the driver can exploit: the off-route segment adds 4.15 km (F4) but the fare's excess-distance line is 4.99 km / $7.04 (F5) and actual GPS distance is +3.0 km (F2); the judge could cap or reshape the refund, and the driver will argue the meter figure is authoritative and unchallengeable.

Speed bands of 20–29 km/h on EU TONG SEN STREET and SENTOSA GATEWAY (F12, F13) let the driver argue there was general slow going, even though those are band 3 and no incident was recorded (F14), so RD-4 (b) is at best corroborative and the argument should be resisted as not reaching the band 1–2 threshold.

Only 1 of the driver's 3 disputes was upheld (F17), so the 'repeated breach' premise for the flag_account request is thin and a judge may find one upheld dispute insufficient to characterise the conduct as repeated.

The covered record shows one off-route segment, 09:04–09:14, driving 5.23 km where the optimal route covers 1.08 km and adding 4.15 km, reaching up to 1989 m off route — too large to be map-matching noise [F4][RD-1]. That segment is not exempt: no traffic incident is recorded near the route in the trip window [F14][RD-4], the only speed bands are band 3 (20–29 km/h) on Eu Tong Sen Street and Sentosa Gateway, i.e. not the band 1–2 congestion bands, and are corroborative at most [F12][F13][RD-4], and the weather was fair [F15][RD-4].

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows one off-route segment 09:04–09:14 in which 5.23 km were driven where the optimal route covers only 1.08 km, adding 4.15 km and reaching up to 1989 m from the optimal route — an unexcused deviation under RD-1.

No exemption applies: there is no traffic incident near the route during the trip window, the only speed-band entries are band 3 (20–29 km/h, not the congested band 1–2) on two roads, and weather was fair, so RD-4 (a) and (b) cannot excuse the segment.

There is no consent to the reroute: the complete, fully timestamped chat contains only the rider's pickup message at 08:47 and the driver's ETA reply at 08:48, both before the 09:04 segment start, and neither mentions any route or road; the driver's post-trip statement that the GPS rerouted him is a claim, not a rider message.

The rider's complaint that the driver never asked before deviating is consistent with the chat record, which shows no route-change proposal from the driver at any time before the 09:04 off-route segment began.

Under RD-2 for a metered RydeTAXI the refund is Σ(unexempted extra_km) × this trip's per-km rate = 4.15 km × $1.4100/km = $5.8515, rounded to $5.85, computed from the off-route extra distance in F4 and the per-km rate in F5.
The driver already has 1 upheld dispute in the last 90 days among 3 disputes, so with this deviation upheld the case becomes 'repeated' and warrants the additional account-review action of RD-6.

weaknesses: The GPS trace ends 4 minutes before the 09:20:45 drop-off (F1), so the final stretch of the journey is not on record — the rival reading of the missing coverage is that it shifts some of the excess distance onto unrecorded ground and may support an 'evidence insufficient / escalate' argument (G12).

There is a discrepancy the driver can exploit: the off-route segment adds 4.15 km (F4) but the fare's excess-distance line is 4.99 km / $7.04 (F5) and actual GPS distance is +3.0 km (F2); the judge could cap or reshape the refund, and the driver will argue the meter figure is authoritative and unchallengeable.

Speed bands of 20–29 km/h on EU TONG SEN STREET and SENTOSA GATEWAY (F12, F13) let the driver argue there was general slow going, even though those are band 3 and no incident was recorded (F14), so RD-4 (b) is at best corroborative and the argument should be resisted as not reaching the band 1–2 threshold.

Only 1 of the driver's 3 disputes was upheld (F17), so the 'repeated breach' premise for the flag_account request is thin and a judge may find one upheld dispute insufficient to characterise the conduct as repeated.

claims.assertion: The meter total the rider complains about is $28.97, of which the fare record attributes $17.16 to 12.17 km of distance; the fare record also shows a distinct excess-distance figure of $7.04 (4.99 km × $1.41/km), so the maximum mileage-linked sum in dispute is $7.04, not the whole fare (F5, F7).

Only one off-route segment is recorded, 09:04–09:14, which covered 5.23 km where the optimal route covers 1.08 km and added 4.15 km; any RD-2 refund can therefore only be computed on that single segment's extra_km (F4).

The driver never recorded a route-change agreement with the rider before the segment: the entire chat consists of two timestamped messages about waiting at the pick-up point and the car's colour, and no message from the rider consents to any reroute, so RD-5 consent is not available to the driver (F8, F9, F10).

The driver's written statement that 'I went where the GPS sent me; it rerouted' was made after the trip and is a claim only, not rider consent; when it conflicts with the chat and GPS records it must yield to them (F11, F10, F4).

The driver has no RD-4 reasonable-cause exemption: the traffic record shows no incidents near the route during the trip window, and the only speed bands recorded (band 3, 20–29 km/h, on Eu Tong Sen Street and Sentosa Gateway) are too mild to show severe congestion, with weather fair and no rain (F12, F13, F14, F15).

Because the detour took the car as far as 1989 m from the optimal route over ten minutes, the segment cannot be characterised as normal map-matching jitter but as an unexplained deviation, so the exemption-free segment stands and RD-1 is breached (F4).

The GPS trace is incomplete, the last sample falling 4 min 0 s before the recorded 09:20:45 drop-off, so the mileage-driven time and distance outside the covered stretch are not on record; the driver's position is that no refund should be computed from an incomplete record (F1).

The driver's 90-day record shows three disputes with one upheld (route: 0, no-show: 0) across 677 trips and a 4.55 rating over a 4.3-year-old account; profile facts may not be used to decide this case, and on a fair reading they do not show a sustained pattern of route deviations (F17).

weaknesses: F4 is the single most damaging fact: a 09:04–09:14 segment covering 5.23 km against 1.08 km optimal, +4.15 km and up to 1989 m off route, is hard to explain as anything but a genuine unexplained deviation under RD-1.
F2 (10.2 km actual vs 7.2 km optimal, +3.0 km / +42%) corroborates the rider's complaint and makes the deviation look material, not marginal.
F5 gives the other side a clean, computable refund figure of $7.04 (4.99 km × $1.41/km), which is likely to be the arithmetic the judge adopts under RD-2.

There is no rider consent message anywhere in the chat (F10, F8, F9), and F11 is only the driver's own post-trip assertion, which under RD-5 and G11 cannot substitute for consent, so the driver has no exemption route.

F14 records no traffic incidents near the route and F12/F13 are only speed band 3 (20–29 km/h), which cannot satisfy RD-4(a) and at most is band 3, functionally useless vs the band 1–2 requirement, so the traffic defence fails.

F1 shows the GPS trace is incomplete; the other side can argue that the fare record F7 (12.17 km billed) plus F5 shows even more distance was billed than the covered trace records, which cuts against the driver on the incomplete-record point.

points.response: Conceded: I do not ask for the whole fare; my claim is limited to the mileage added by the unexempted segment, and I accept the driver's own arithmetic cap that the mile-linked sum in dispute is $7.04 (F5, F7).

Agreed that only the single 09:04–09:14 segment is recorded and that RD-2 refunds are computed per unexempted segment; the dispute is purely over the correct multiplier for that segment's extra_km (F4).
Agreed: the complete, all-timestamped chat contains no rider message about any route at all, so the driver has no RD-5 consent (F8, F9, F10).
Agreed: the post-trip statement 'I went where the GPS sent me; it rerouted' is a bare claim by the driver which yields to the chat and GPS records and cannot create consent (F11, F10, F4).

Agreed: no traffic incident is recorded near the route in the trip window and the only bands are band 3 (20–29 km/h) with fair weather, so the RD-4 reasonable-cause exemption fails (F12, F13, F14, F15).
Agreed: a deviation reaching 1989 m from the optimal route over ten minutes cannot be map-matching noise, so the segment is an unexplained deviation and RD-1 is breached (F4).

The incomplete trace does not help the driver: RD-2 refunds the distance units actually charged, and F4 plus the fare record F5/F7 already establish that the unexempted segment was driven and billed inside the covered stretch, so no unrecorded mileage needs to be assumed (F1, F4, F5, F7).

I accept profile facts cannot decide the case, but the segment itself is upheld on F4, and RD-6 only requires the 90-day history as the additional trigger — F17 shows 1 upheld dispute already in that window, making this case 'repeated' (F4, F17).

I revise my own quantum claim: the RD-2 refund should be 4.99 km × $1.4100/km = $7.04 as shown in F5, rather than the 4.15 km figure I first computed from F4, because that is the mileage-linked amount actually billed for the unexempted deviation (F5, F4).

Conceded as to segment existence: the GPS record does show the 09:04–09:14 off-route stretch of 5.23 km against 1.08 km optimal, and the driver does not dispute that it is the only recorded deviation (F4). The driver's position is limited to quantum — the segment's extra_km is 4.15 km (F4), and that is the only figure RD-2 permits.

Not contested: F14 records no incidents near the route in the trip window, F12/F13 are band 3 (20–29 km/h) rather than the band 1–2 severe-congestion bands, and F15 shows fair weather, so RD-4(a) fails and RD-4(b) is corroborative only — the driver is not claiming a reasonable-cause exemption.

Agreed on the consent point, and the driver accepts that the rider never sent a message consenting to any route: the chat is two timestamped messages with no route or road mentioned (F8, F9, F10), and F11 is the driver's own post-trip statement, which under RD-5 is a claim, not consent. Note this cuts only against consent, not against the amount owed.

Conceded: since the chat is complete and timestamped (F10) and contains no route proposal before the 09:04 segment start recorded in F4, the driver cannot show he asked first, so there is no RD-5 consent for that segment.

The $5.85 figure is wrong arithmetic: RD-2 refunds the unexempted segment's own extra_km of 4.15 km (F4) at the per-km rate of $1.4100 from the fare record, which is $5.85 only if one reads the segment term alone — but the fare record separately bills 4.99 km of excess distance at that same $1.41 rate, $7.04, and RD-2 refunds only mileage units actually billed, so the refund cannot exceed the $7.04 excess-distance line and the driver asks the court to adopt $7.04 as the computation base or the lower of the two (F4, F5).

The flag_account request rests on profile facts alone: F17 shows three disputes with exactly one upheld and a route-specific count of zero, and RD-6 additionally requires that this case be one where a refund is payable; even then the profile fact may only support an ancillary action and never the finding itself, and one upheld dispute in 90 days is not a pattern of route breaches (F17).

The driver does not withdraw the incomplete-GPS point but does not press it to block a ruling: F1 shows the trace stops 4 min 0 s before the 09:20:45 drop-off, so the unrecorded final stretch is not chargeable to the driver as an extra unexcused deviation, and the segment in F4 remains the only basis for any refund.
